found.domain: healthcare-prior-auth-and-claims (US prior authorisation / utilisation management, payer medical policy, claims edits, denials and appeals, coding disputes, peer-to-peer; France CPAM accord préalable as comparator)

workflows.name: Prior authorisation medical-necessity determinations (payer side, US Medicare Advantage + commercial)
workflows.geography: US (Medicare Advantage best-measured; commercial and Medicaid managed care similar)
workflows.decision_volume: ~53 million PA determinations in Medicare Advantage alone in 2024 (KFF analysis of CMS data, https://www.kff.org/medicare/medicare-advantage-insurers-made-nearly-53-million-prior-authorization-determinations-in-2024/ , academic/foundation, sourced). ~4.1-4.2 million denied (8%). AHIP 2024 member survey: only ~7% of commercial medical claims are subject to PA at all (https://ahiporg-production.s3.amazonaws.com/documents/202506_AHIP_Report_Prior_Authorization.pdf , industry association, fetched). Commercial/Medicaid volume not found as a national number.
workflows.human_review_rate: Two-tier: ~92% of MA requests approved (KFF, CMS data); AHIP reports 97-98% of medical-service PAs ultimately approved and only ~20% approved in real time, i.e. roughly 80% touch a nurse/clinician at some point (AHIP PDF, industry association). AuthDenied's aggregation of CY2025 CMS-0057-F disclosures: median contract denial 7.2%, request-weighted 9.0%, range 2.3%-32.7% by insurer (https://www.authdenied.com/insights/medicare-advantage-denial-rates-by-insurer , vendor aggregator of regulator-mandated disclosures). Physician (medical-director) review is legally required for every medical-necessity denial (California SB 1120, AHIP commitment, CMS-4201-F), so 100% of the ~8% denial stream is human-reviewed by a physician.
workflows.why_humans_review: Rough estimate (not sourced as a breakdown): A missing evidence 35-45% (AHIP states initial denials are 'often a result of incomplete information from providers'; P2P overturns of nearly 100% for orthopaedic CT/MRI denials (Orthopedics 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37921528/) and 80.7% appeal overturn (KFF) imply the initial file lacked what the criteria needed); B factual classification against MCG/InterQual/plan criteria 25-35% (nurse first-level review is criteria matching; nurses cannot deny, only refer up); C rule interpretation 5-10%; D conflict of authorities 5-10% (OIG 2022: 13% of sampled MA PA denials met Medicare coverage rules, chiefly because MAOs applied internal clinical criteria not contained in Medicare rules, https://oig.hhs.gov/reports/all/2022/some-medicare-advantage-organization-denials-of-prior-authorization-requests-raise-concerns-about-beneficiary-access-to-medically-necessary-care/ ; CMS-4201-F then settled this conflict by regulation); E true clinical discretion 10-15% (medical director judgment on criteria-not-met cases; regulation deliberately keeps this human); H repeatable ambiguity settled prospectively 3-8% (criteria silent: new technology, off-label, 'not fully established' coverage; these route to medical policy / technology assessment committees, see medical policy workflow). G and F negligible. Basis: AHIP survey statement, OIG sample, overturn rates, structure of two-level UM (StatPearls/NCBI UM chapter, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560806/ ). Wide inter-insurer denial variation (2.3%-32.7%) suggests much 'interpretation' is really plan policy choice, not unsettled ambiguity.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: Medicare Advantage rule CMS-4201-F (42 CFR 422.101(b)(6), 422.137): when Medicare coverage criteria are 'not fully established', an MAO may create internal coverage criteria, but they must be publicly accessible, evidence-based, and reviewed annually by a Utilization Management Committee; MA plans must otherwise follow NCDs/LCDs and the two-midnight rule. This is a regulator-imposed settlement loop: the recurring ambiguity (MAO criteria vs Medicare rules, flagged by OIG) was settled by rule and internal settlements must be written down as versioned public criteria.
settlement_loop_evidence.source_type: regulator (via law-firm summary; CMS FAQ Feb 2024; cms.gov and ecfr.gov blocked)
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Internal coverage criteria become published policy with effective dates; UM committee annual review; applies to all later requests.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: Health plan medical technology assessment committees: 'as soon as the Committee has knowledge of a new technology... it seeks to develop a policy'; requests come from claims personnel, medical directors, account executives; 1996 JGIM survey of US plans: medical directors participate in policy review in 96% of plans but have final coverage authority in only 27% (committee-owned settlement).
settlement_loop_evidence.source_type: academic (J Gen Intern Med 1996) plus Kaiser Permanente WA MTAC page https://wa-provider.kaiserpermanente.org/clinical-review/mtac (payer documentation)
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Committee decision becomes a written medical policy applied to subsequent requests; individual pre-policy cases decided by medical director.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: Payer customisation of licensed criteria: plans publish 'Customization to Care Guidelines' documents per MCG edition and 'reserve the right to review and modify' MCG/InterQual criteria; plan clinical UM guidelines supersede MCG/InterQual (Wellpoint provider site).
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Custom criteria versioned by MCG edition and applied by nurses at first-level review; this is the existing 'executable settlement' mechanism.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: NCQA UM accreditation requires periodic inter-rater reliability testing of nurses and medical directors against criteria (consistency mechanism, not settlement capture); Louisiana Medicaid MCO IRR policy and Arizona DCS policy set testing frequency and pass thresholds.
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Detects inconsistency between reviewers; does not itself record a binding interpretation.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: Gold-card laws (Texas HB 3459, 2021 and 2025 amendments): a physician with >=90% approval on >=5 requests over 6 months is exempted from PA for that service; re-evaluated each 6 months. Settlement is at the provider level (trust), not the interpretation level.
settlement_loop_evidence.source_type: industry association (Texas Medical Association) + payer FAQ https://www.uhcprovider.com/content/dam/provider/docs/public/health-plans/tx-commercial-gold-card-faq.pdf
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Prospective exemption for 6 months; automatically recomputed from data; no interpretation captured.

workflows.economic_pain: Provider side: AMA Dec-2024 survey of 1,000 physicians: 39 PAs per physician per week, 13 staff-hours per week, 40% have staff working exclusively on PA (https://www.ama-assn.org/system/files/prior-authorization-survey.pdf , industry association). CAQH 2024 Index: manual PA costs providers $10.97 vs $5.79 electronic, 24 minutes per manual PA (https://www.caqh.org/hubfs/Index/2024%20Index%20Report/CAQH%202024%20Index%20Report%20Key%20Takeaways%20FINAL.pdf , industry body; figures via search snippets, PDF blocked). Payer side: $3.41 manual vs $0.05 automated per transaction (HealthEdge blog citing CAQH, vendor, https://healthedge.com/resources/blog/how-health-plans-can-improve-outcomes-and-reduce-costs-with-automated-prior-authorizations). Physician reviewer labour: $75/case low end, $100-180/hour UR physicians, IRO contract $85-110/hour (press/career sites, weak). Error cost: 80.7% of appealed MA denials overturned but only ~12% appealed (KFF); OIG 2026: LTCH 65% and IRF 54% denial rates at 19 largest MAOs, overturns >80% at some plans (https://oig.hhs.gov/documents/audit/11693/OEI-09-24-00330.pdf , inspector general). Wrong-decision cost is mostly patient harm/delay and regulatory exposure, not payer leakage.
workflows.existing_solutions: Criteria: MCG (Hearst) and InterQual (Optum) licensed criteria with plan customisation; plan medical policies / clinical policy bulletins (Aetna CPB, Cigna, Anthem CUMG). UM platforms: HealthEdge GuidingCare, Cohere Health (claims 85-90% auto-approval, 'expert digitization' of plan policies into rules, https://www.coherehealth.com/news/intelligent-prior-authorization-overwhelming-auto-approval-rate , vendor), Availity AuthAI, Anterior, Latent/Latitude, Alaffia (agents matching records to plan criteria), Waystar (6.8M payer rules, provider side). Standards: HL7 Da Vinci CRD/DTR/PAS express payer documentation rules as FHIR Questionnaires with executable CQL (fetched: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HL7/davinci-dtr/master/input/pagecontent/index.md). Do they capture settlements as versioned executable precedents? Partially: medical policies and MCG customisations are versioned by edition with effective dates and are executed by nurses/rules, so the settlement-to-rule path exists and is owned by medical policy departments; what is not evidenced is a per-case ledger linking an escalated case to the policy change it produced.
workflows.buyer_and_budget: Payer: VP Utilization Management / Chief Medical Officer / Medical Policy director; budget exists (UM platforms, Cohere-type vendors funded at scale; Alaffia raised $55M in 2026, press). Provider: revenue-cycle VP, but they buy submission automation not interpretation capture.
workflows.regulatory_constraints: Strong: CMS-4201-F (MA must follow Medicare criteria, public internal criteria, UM committee), CMS-0057-F (72h/7-day turnaround from 2026, APIs and public metrics by 2027), California SB 1120 (licensed physician must make every medical-necessity denial; AI may not autonomously deny), AHIP June-2025 commitment that all medical-necessity denials are clinician-reviewed, gold-card laws in TX and other states. Net effect: approvals may be automated, denials must stay human, so precedent cannot remove the physician from the exact decision class where interpretation matters (brief's H4 penalty).
workflows.notes: Volume and cost are large and well measured, but the addressable share for a settlement-capture product is small: most human touches are missing evidence (A) or criteria matching (B), the truly interpretive residue is legally reserved to physicians (E), and the recurring interpretive gaps (new technology, criteria not fully established) already flow into a formal, regulated, versioned medical-policy process (H3 holds). CMS-4201-F is itself an example of a regulator settling the biggest recurring ambiguity (MAO criteria vs Medicare rules) by rule.

workflows.name: Payer medical policy / clinical coverage policy formation and maintenance
workflows.decision_volume: Per plan: hundreds of medical policies (Anthem, Aetna CPBs, Cigna coverage policies); update cadence monthly to quarterly (payer policy update bulletins). Count of policies changed per year not found. Medicare FFS analogue: LCD reconsideration requests to MACs (volume per year not found), NCDs. This is the low-volume settlement layer sitting above ~53M MA PA decisions.
workflows.human_review_rate: 100% of policy decisions are committee/human decisions by design (technology assessment committees, P&T committees, UM committee annual review under 42 CFR 422.137). 1996 JGIM survey: medical directors take part in 96% of plans' new-technology review (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8725978/ , academic).
workflows.why_humans_review: Estimate: H 40-60% (deciding a coverage position for a recurring class: new technology, off-label use, level-of-care threshold) - this is exactly the brief's category H; C 15-25% (interpreting NCD/LCD language for the plan); D 10-20% (reconciling MCG/InterQual with plan benefits and Medicare rules); E 10-15% (evidence-grading judgment). Basis: committee descriptions (Kaiser WA MTAC, Priority Health policy 91430, PacificSource new-technology policy), CMS-4201-F requirements; no quantitative breakdown exists.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: Anthem policy ADMIN.00001 'Medical Policy Formation' documents the formal process by which individual coverage questions become versioned medical policies (page blocked; title and existence confirmed via search).
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Policy with number, version and effective date applied by UM staff prospectively.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: PacificSource and Priority Health 'New and Emerging Technology' policies define how a request with no existing policy is handled (medical director case decision, then technology assessment and policy creation) - the pre-policy case is settled individually and the class is then codified.
settlement_loop_evidence.source_type: payer documentation (also https://www.priorityhealth.com/-/media/priorityhealth/documents/medical-policies/91430.pdf); pages blocked, content known only from titles/snippets
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Coverage status list updated for the technology; later requests decided from the list.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: Medicare FFS: LCD reconsideration process lets stakeholders request revision of a Local Coverage Determination; MAC must validate within 60 days; proposed LCD, public comment, Contractor Advisory Committee, final LCD. HHS Departmental Appeals Board may designate Medicare Appeals Council decisions as precedential (42 CFR 401.109, 2017 rule) binding on ALJs, QICs and MACs.
settlement_loop_evidence.source_type: regulator (CMS Program Integrity Manual ch.13; 42 CFR 401.109 at https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-A/part-401/subpart-B/section-401.109)
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: LCDs and precedential Council decisions bind future determinations; number of precedential designations not found (believed very small).

settlement_loop_evidence.description: France: HAS-validated référentiels fix, for 14 rehabilitation situations, the number of physiotherapy sessions reimbursable without accord préalable, converting a recurring case-by-case medical-service judgment into a bright-line rule.
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Threshold rules replace individual prior agreement below the threshold.

workflows.economic_pain: Not quantified in public sources. Indirect: OIG 2022 estimated ~85,000 improper MA PA denials per year partly from plan criteria diverging from Medicare rules (press summaries of OIG, https://www.healthcarefinancenews.com/news/medicare-advantage-plans-deny-prior-authorizations-meet-medicare-approval-oig-says); CMS-4201-F compliance forced re-review of all internal criteria. Labour is a small medical-policy team per plan (headcount not found).
workflows.existing_solutions: In-house medical policy committees; MCG/InterQual editions with plan customisation; policy authoring/publishing tools (Cotiviti Payment Policy Management for payment policies, https://resources.cotiviti.com/payment-integrity/payment-policy-management-solution , vendor); Cohere 'policy digitization' services; document management. Settlements ARE captured as versioned prospective policy text; execution happens via nurse review or vendor rule configuration. Missing (not evidenced either way): a structured ledger from triggering cases to policy versions.
workflows.buyer_and_budget: Chief Medical Officer / VP Medical Policy at a health plan; small team; budget modest; long, compliance-driven sales cycle.
workflows.regulatory_constraints: 42 CFR 422.101(b)(6) and 422.137 (public criteria, UM committee annual review, physician expertise); state UR laws; NCQA UM standards (annual criteria review, IRR).
workflows.notes: This is the one workflow in the cluster where category H dominates and the settlement loop is formal, owned and prospective. But it is low-volume (hundreds of policies per plan) and already institutionalised in committees, editions and policy documents, so the brief's H3 (already encoded adequately) and H8 (small labour pool) both bite. A product would be a policy-lifecycle/case-to-policy ledger feature inside UM platforms, not a standalone category.

workflows.name: Claims edits, denials and appeals (provider-payer, US)
workflows.decision_volume: Premier 2024 survey: ~15% of claims to private payers initially denied (MA 15.7%, managed Medicaid 15.1%, Medicaid 16.7%, Medicare FFS 8.4%) (https://premierinc.com/newsroom/policy/claims-adjudication-costs-providers-257-billion-18-billion-is-potentially-unnecessary-expense , industry group/GPO survey; page blocked, figures from press). National claim count not stated; at billions of claims per year this implies hundreds of millions of denials. Provider cost $25.7B for 2023 claims adjudication, ~$18B 'potentially unnecessary'.
workflows.human_review_rate: Every denied claim is worked manually by provider staff at $57.23 average admin cost per denied claim in 2023 (up from $43.84 in 2022) (Premier via press). ~70% of denials ultimately overturned and paid (Premier). Change Healthcare 2022 Denials Index: 86% of denials potentially avoidable (https://blr.postclickmarketing.com/Global/FileLib/HLM/2022-revenue-cycle-denials-index.pdf , vendor).
workflows.why_humans_review: Estimate from the Change Healthcare Denials Index cause mix: A/B missing or wrong data 50-60% (registration/eligibility 26.6%, authorisation/precert missing 11.6%, plus documentation requests); C rule interpretation 15-25% (service not covered 10.6%, coding/bundling/modifier edits, medical-necessity edits); D conflict of authorities 5-10% (plan reimbursement policy vs CPT/NCCI/Coding Clinic guidance); F commercial negotiation 5-10% (contract disputes, DRG downgrades resolved by contract amendment); H repeatable ambiguity 5-15% (E/M leveling, modifier 25/59, sepsis and other clinical-validation definitions, observation vs inpatient) - recurring and in practice settled by contract language or payer policy updates; E small. Basis: Denials Index category shares (vendor), sepsis-definition literature, two-midnight rule history.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: Sepsis clinical-validation disputes: payers apply Sepsis-3 (SOFA >=2) while clinicians document under Sepsis-2; a Critical Care Explorations paper ('Sepsis-2.5') proposes a negotiated definition to resolve payer-provider conflict; DRG downgrade overturns recover $3,000-7,000 per claim. Same ambiguity recurs across thousands of claims and is settled, when at all, by contract language.
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Contract clause fixing the definition applies to all future claims between that hospital and payer; but is bilateral (F), not an interpretation ledger.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: AHA Coding Clinic for ICD-10-CM/PCS: coders submit questions to the AHA Central Office; answers approved unanimously by the Cooperating Parties are published quarterly (e.g. 28 Q&As in Q2 2025, 23 in Q2 2026) and are authoritative and prospective. A canonical industry-level settlement loop for coding ambiguity.
settlement_loop_evidence.source_type: industry association (AHA); page blocked, details via https://www.aapc.com/codify/coding-clinic-icd-10.aspx and https://www.codingclinicadvisor.com/blog/what-ahas-coding-clinic-second-quarter-2025-release-icd-10-cm-and-icd-10-pcs
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Published advice binds coding from the effective date; ~100 settlements per year industry-wide, i.e. the loop exists but at tiny volume relative to disputes.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: Payer reimbursement/payment policies and clinical claim edits (ClaimsXten, Cotiviti Payment Policy Management) are maintained as versioned rule libraries sourced from CMS/AMA guidance and plan-customised; provider dispute processes (Cigna, Aetna) allow reconsideration when a coding edit is challenged.
settlement_loop_evidence.source_type: vendor (Cotiviti) and payer documentation (https://chk.static.cigna.com/assets/chcp/resourceLibrary/clinicalReimbursementPayment/medicalClinicalReimbursePoliciesProcedures.html); both blocked, from snippets
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Edits are executable rules with versions; whether individual dispute outcomes feed edit retirement is not evidenced.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: Two-midnight rule (2013) is a regulator settlement of the recurring inpatient-vs-observation ambiguity; CMS-4201-F extended it to MA in 2024, yet hospitals still run daily physician-advisor secondary reviews of observation cases and improvement projects target moving appropriate-status rates from 76% to 90%.
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Bright-line rule; residual ambiguity ('expectation' of two midnights) still needs per-case physician judgment, showing settlement does not eliminate E.

workflows.economic_pain: $57.23 per denied claim, $25.7B provider adjudication cost, ~$18B potentially unnecessary (Premier, industry survey via press). Clinical-validation DRG downgrades $3-7k per claim (vendor). Payer side: payment-integrity vendors monetise edits at scale (Alaffia $55M raise, press https://medcitynews.com/2026/02/alaffia-health-insurance-funding-capital-claims/).
workflows.existing_solutions: Payer: ClaimsXten (Change/Optum), Cotiviti, Optum CES; policy libraries versioned. Provider: Epic Resolute denial workqueues, Waystar, R1/Ensemble/CorroHealth outsourced denial teams, physician advisor programs; payer-rule knowledge often held in spreadsheets (not evidenced quantitatively, search budget exhausted). Industry: AHA Coding Clinic, AMA CPT Assistant, NCCI policy manual. Settlements as versioned executable precedents: yes on the payer edit side; no evidence of a case-to-rule ledger on the provider side.
workflows.buyer_and_budget: Provider: VP Revenue Cycle / Denials Director (large budgets, outsourcing common). Payer: VP Payment Integrity. Both already spend heavily with incumbents.
workflows.regulatory_constraints: Appeal timelines (ERISA, state prompt-pay and dispute laws, MA reconsideration rules); HIPAA transaction standards; no rule prohibits automating provider-side appeal logic.
workflows.notes: Recurrence of interpretive disputes is real (sepsis, E/M, modifiers, status), but the majority of denial labour is missing/incorrect data, and the recurring interpretive classes are settled either bilaterally in contracts (F) or by industry bodies at very low settlement volume. Incumbents already hold versioned rule libraries. Could be a wedge only on the provider side as 'payer-specific interpretation playbook', where H3 is weaker; evidence for that gap is anecdotal.

workflows.name: Peer-to-peer reviews and appeals of PA denials (provider vs payer medical director)
workflows.decision_volume: MA: ~12% of ~4.1M denials appealed in 2024 (~0.5M appeals), 80.7% overturned (KFF). CY2025 CMS-0057-F disclosures: 6.2% of denials appealed, 75.2% overturned (AuthDenied aggregation, vendor). P2P volume not published; AMA survey: only 16% of physicians say the P2P reviewer is often/always qualified.
workflows.human_review_rate: 100% by construction (physician-to-physician call or physician reconsideration).
workflows.why_humans_review: Estimate: A missing evidence 50-70% (near-100% P2P approval for ortho CT/MRI, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37921528/ academic; 'documentation reaching a reviewer for the first time' is the most common overturn driver per vendor guides); E discretion 20-30%; C 5-10%; H <5%. Basis: overturn rates so high that the initial denial was rarely a settled interpretation.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: California DMHC Independent Medical Review: 2,838 IMRs resolved in 2023, 72.7% overturned; ~3,478 in 2024 with ~70% overturned; Anthem 863 IMRs of which 688 medical necessity, 68.6% overturned. Workers' comp IMR (separate, criteria-bound MTUS) overturned only 10.2% of UR denials in 2023. IMR decisions are case-specific and not precedential.
settlement_loop_evidence.source_type: regulator (CA DIR) and DMHC data via https://data.chhs.ca.gov/dataset/independent-medical-review-imr-determinations-trend and law-firm summary https://www.gmlawyers.com/dmhc-imr-data/ (all blocked; numbers from snippets)
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Not reused; the contrast (10% overturn where criteria are codified in a statutory schedule vs ~70% where plan criteria apply) is itself evidence that codified criteria collapse discretion.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: OIG 2026: MAOs overturned nearly all appealed SNF admission denials, 'raising concerns about initial denials'; no mechanism found by which those overturns change the plan's criteria.
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: Overturns are case-specific; regulator pressure, not a ledger, drives criteria change.

workflows.economic_pain: Provider physician time per P2P (not sourced; vendor guides say 15-30 minutes); payer physician reviewer $75/case to $180/hour (press). IMR fee $560 per single-physician review (CA DIR 2013 schedule, regulator).
workflows.existing_solutions: Phone calls, fax, payer portals; provider-side denial vendors (Muni, Counterforce, Linear) generating appeal letters; IROs (MRIoA etc.).
workflows.buyer_and_budget: Provider practice managers; low willingness to pay per P2P.
workflows.regulatory_constraints: P2P and appeal rights fixed by CMS and state law; physician must decide.
workflows.notes: Outcomes are case-specific, driven by evidence supply and physician discretion, and explicitly non-precedential. Fails the brief's H4 and the 'decisions are mostly one-off' penalty.

workflows.name: France: CPAM/MSA accord préalable (entente préalable) and service médical avis
workflows.decision_volume: National count of demandes d'accord préalable not found. Structure: silence for 15 days (21 if complex) equals acceptance, so only refusals are decisions (https://www.ameli.fr/assure/remboursements/etre-bien-rembourse/accord-prealable , public insurer). Medical appeals: 8,787 CMRA recours in 2023 (+15% vs 2022) (law-firm blog https://www.mgdc-avocats.fr/fr/actualites/id-431-la-commission-medicale-de-recours-amiable , weak). Staffing example: DRSM Bretagne 2024: 64 médecins-conseils, 9 chirurgiens-dentistes conseils, 8 pharmaciens conseils, 21 infirmiers (https://rapport-annuel.assurance-maladie.fr/drsm-bretagne/chiffres-cles , public insurer annual report).
workflows.human_review_rate: Unknown; refusals require a médecin-conseil avis; Cour des comptes 2025: a-posteriori controls cover only 0.1% of payments, control of coverage conditions judged insufficient (https://www.whatsupdoc-lemag.fr/article/prescriptions-indemnites-journalieres-teleconsultation-ce-que-la-cour-des-comptes-dit , press summarising the audit body).
workflows.why_humans_review: Estimate: A 30-40%, B 20-30%, E 20-30% (médecin-conseil clinical opinion), H 5-10% (HAS référentiels and MSAP thresholds show the recurring classes are settled by national rule). Basis: HAS kiné référentiels (14 situations), MSAP mechanism; no statistics.

settlement_loop_evidence.description: HAS référentiels de rééducation fix the number of physiotherapy sessions per indication that need no accord préalable; MSAP (mise sous accord préalable) targets outlier prescribers/establishments for SSR admissions and transports based on data.
settlement_loop_evidence.reusable_how: National bright-line thresholds; settlement happens at HAS/CNAM level, not at caisse level.

workflows.economic_pain: Not quantified publicly; the Cour des comptes frames the problem as under-control (too little review), the opposite of the brief's over-review pain.
workflows.existing_solutions: CNAM internal systems, national doctrine from CNAM/HAS; monopoly public buyer.
workflows.buyer_and_budget: CNAM (single public buyer, procurement-bound); not a realistic early customer.
workflows.regulatory_constraints: Code de la sécurité sociale; silence = acceptance; CMRA mandatory pre-litigation; RGPD/health data.
workflows.notes: Deemed-approval design and a single public buyer make this unattractive; recurring ambiguity is settled by national référentiels, i.e. by the regulator, not by local decision owners.

evidence_against_thesis: H1 supported: the industry's own statement is that initial PA denials are 'often a result of incomplete information from providers' (AHIP 2024 survey, fetched PDF) and Change Healthcare's Denials Index puts registration/eligibility (26.6%) and authorisation (11.6%) at the top of claim-denial causes; 80-100% overturn rates on appeal/P2P (KFF, OIG 2026, Orthopedics 2023) indicate the original decision lacked facts rather than a settled interpretation.

H4 supported strongly: California SB 1120, the AHIP June-2025 commitment and CMS MA rules require a licensed physician to make every medical-necessity denial and forbid autonomous AI denial; precedent cannot legally remove the human from the exact decision class where interpretation lives. Automation is permitted only for approvals, which vendors already do (Cohere claims 85-90% auto-approval).

H3 supported: the settlement loop already exists in institutionalised form: medical policy committees producing numbered, versioned, effective-dated policies; MCG/InterQual editions with plan customisation documents; CMS-4201-F forcing internal criteria to be public and reviewed annually by a UM committee; AHA Coding Clinic and LCD reconsideration at industry/regulator level; Da Vinci DTR expressing payer rules as executable CQL.

H2 partially supported: where the loop is formal (Coding Clinic ~100 Q&As/year; precedential Medicare Appeals Council decisions; new-technology policies) settlement volume is tiny compared with tens of millions of decisions; the high-volume residue is discretion or evidence, not new settleable ambiguity.

The biggest recurring 'ambiguity' in MA (plan criteria stricter than Medicare rules, OIG 2022: 13% of denials met Medicare rules) was a policy choice by plans, settled by regulation (CMS-4201-F), not by a missing capture tool; and inter-insurer denial rates spanning 2.3%-32.7% (CY2025 disclosures) show variation is driven by plan strategy rather than uncaptured interpretation.

Where criteria are fully codified by statute (California workers' comp MTUS), IMR overturn is 10.2%; where plan criteria apply, IMR overturn is ~70%: codification works, but it is done by legislatures and payers with existing tools, again pointing to H3.

H8 for the pure H layer: medical-policy teams are small per plan; the large labour pools (UM nurses, denial staff) are doing A/B work already targeted by incumbent automation vendors (Cohere, Availity, Anterior, Alaffia, Waystar).
not_found: Share of first-level nurse reviews escalated to physician reviewers (payer side) and physician reviewer cases per day
Number of medical policies created/updated per plan per year and medical-policy team headcount
Count of precedential Medicare Appeals Council decisions designated since 2017 and LCD reconsideration requests per year
National volume of French demandes d'accord préalable and refusal rate; CNAM médecins-conseils national headcount

Any quantitative breakdown of PA denial reasons into missing documentation vs criteria not met vs no applicable policy (Commonwealth Fund '24% medical necessity' figure seen only second-hand in a vendor blog)
Commercial (non-MA) national PA volume and denial/overturn rates

found.domain_assessment: Overall: weak evidence for a standalone Sophon-shaped product in healthcare prior auth and claims, with one moderate pocket. The cluster has the volume (53M MA PA decisions/year, 15% initial claim denial rates, $25.7B provider adjudication cost) and the cost per decision ($3-11 per PA, $57 per denied claim, $75+ per physician review), but the human labour is dominated by missing evidence and criteria matching (AHIP: denials 'often a result of incomplete information'; 26.6% of claim denials are registration/eligibility; 80-100% overturn rates once records arrive), and the interpretive residue is legally reserved to physicians (SB 1120, AHIP pledge, CMS rules) so precedent cannot displace the reviewer on denials. The settlement loop the brief asks for genuinely exists here, but it is already institutionalised and versioned: medical policy committees and technology assessment committees produce numbered, effective-dated policies; MCG/InterQual editions carry plan customisations; CMS-4201-F forces internal coverage criteria into public, annually reviewed documents; AHA Coding Clinic and LCD reconsideration settle industry-level ambiguity prospectively; Da Vinci DTR encodes payer rules as executable CQL. That is direct support for H3 and H4, and the settlement volume in the formal loops is tiny relative to decision volume (support for H2). The most Sophon-like pocket is recurring payer-provider interpretive disputes in claims (sepsis and other clinical-validation definitions, E/M leveling, modifiers, inpatient status) that get settled bilaterally by contract or policy update and recur across thousands of claims; a provider-side 'payer interpretation playbook' with provenance is plausible but evidence for the gap is anecdotal and incumbents (Cotiviti, ClaimsXten, Epic, Waystar, outsourced denial firms) are strong. France is negative (deemed approval by silence, single public buyer, ambiguity settled by HAS référentiels). Caveats: the egress proxy blocked nearly all primary pages (KFF, OIG, CMS, CAQH, AMA, Premier, eCFR), so most numbers rest on search snippets of those sources; only the AHIP report and the HL7 Da Vinci GitHub pages were fetched in full; the WebSearch budget was exhausted before confirming Texas gold-card uptake, Coding Clinic inquiry volumes and French DAP volumes. Recommendation for the parent: do not pick this cluster as the wedge; if any experiment is run here, sample ~200 hospital denial-appeal cases at one health system and classify whether the winning argument was new evidence (A), criteria match (B) or a reusable payer-specific interpretation (H) - the prior evidence suggests H will be under 10%.

verification.domain: healthcare-prior-auth-and-claims (US prior authorisation / utilisation management, payer medical policy, claims denials and appeals, peer-to-peer; France accord préalable). VERIFIER NETWORK NOTE: this session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200/200) when the verification began, and the egress proxy blocked every non-GitHub host attempted (kff.org, oig.hhs.gov, premierinc.com, pubmed, europepmc, govinfo.gov, ecfr.gov, hhs.gov, leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, ama-assn.org, caqh.org, ncqa.org, ameli.fr, texmed.org, tdi.texas.gov, authdenied.com, commonwealthfund.org, mcdermottlaw.com, wellpoint, hallrender.com, aha.org, plus ~50 probed API/data hosts). The GitHub search API returned 503/502. Verification therefore rests on (a) the AHIP June-2025 PDF, which I downloaded and whose text I checked against the finder's own saved extraction (scratchpad/ahip_pa.txt), (b) the HL7 Da Vinci DTR/PAS pages on raw.githubusercontent.com, and (c) my background knowledge of the cited primary sources, with confidence stated per item. Anything I could not check is marked unverified, not refuted.

refuted.claim: "~20% approved in real time, i.e. roughly 80% touch a nurse/clinician at some point" (PA workflow, human_review_rate)
refuted.why: The AHIP PDF (verified text) says only that 'approximately 20% of prior authorizations for medical services are approved in real-time'. It does not say the remaining 80% are reviewed by a nurse or clinician. Non-real-time approvals include batch/auto-adjudicated approvals, approvals pended for eligibility or benefit checks, and requests submitted by fax/phone (45%) that are keyed in before an automated rules pass. The 80% human-touch figure is the finder's inference, not AHIP's statement, and is presented as sourced. The honest statement is: human-touch rate for medical PA is unknown; the only sourced bounds are >=~3% (final denials, which must be clinician-reviewed) and <=~80%.

refuted.claim: "100% of the ~8% denial stream is human-reviewed by a physician" (4.1-4.2M physician decisions/year in MA)
refuted.why: Physician review is required only for adverse medical-necessity determinations (42 CFR 422.566(d); SB 1120; the AHIP commitment text I verified says 'all prior authorization denials based on medical necessity for clinical factors will be reviewed by a licensed and qualified clinician'). KFF's MA denial counts include administrative and benefit denials (non-covered service, out-of-network, duplicate, missing information, partial approvals), which do not require a physician. So the physician-reviewed stream is some unknown fraction of the ~4.2M denials, not all of it; the 4.2M figure overstates the physician-labour pool that a precedent product could touch.

refuted.claim: Sepsis clinical-validation settlement: "a Critical Care Explorations paper ('Sepsis-2.5') proposes a negotiated definition... settled, when at all, by contract language" listed as prospective=yes settlement-loop evidence
refuted.why: A journal article proposing a compromise definition is not evidence that any organisation has settled the ambiguity; the finder's own wording ('proposes', 'when at all') concedes this. Where sepsis definitions are fixed bilaterally in payer-provider contracts, the settlement is a negotiated commercial term (brief category F) between two parties, made by contracting staff, not an interpretation ledger inside one institution. As settlement-loop evidence for the mechanism this item should be scored prospective='no evidence' rather than 'yes'.

refuted.claim: "Every denied claim is worked manually by provider staff at $57.23 average admin cost per denied claim"
refuted.why: Premier's figure (industry survey, unverifiable here) is an average cost per denied claim among reworked claims; it does not establish that every denied claim is worked. Revenue-cycle practice writes off low-dollar denials without rework (the same Premier release and the Change Healthcare index frame a large share of denials as never appealed/recovered). 'Every' is unsupported.

weakened.claim: AHIP: initial denials are 'often a result of incomplete information from providers' used as support for H1 (missing facts dominate)
weakened.why: Verified as an exact quote in the AHIP June-2025 PDF, but it is an unquantified assertion by the payer trade association in an advocacy document, with an obvious incentive to attribute denials to providers. OIG 2022 (OEI-09-18-00260, from background knowledge, not fetched) found that among denials meeting Medicare rules the MAOs had requested documentation that was already in the file, i.e. some 'incomplete information' is payer-constructed rather than genuinely missing. H1 support should rest on the appeal/P2P overturn rates and the Change Healthcare cause mix, not on the AHIP sentence. Net: H1 still supported, but by weaker evidence than the finder implies.

weakened.claim: KFF: ~53M MA PA determinations 2024, ~8% denied, ~12% appealed, 80.7% overturned
weakened.why: Could not fetch (kff.org blocked). Consistent with KFF's published series (2023: ~49.8M determinations, 6.4% denied, 11.7% appealed, 81.7% overturned) and internally arithmetically consistent, so plausible, but unverified this session. Treat as moderate-confidence sourced.

weakened.claim: OIG 2022: 13% of sampled MA PA denials met Medicare coverage rules; ~85,000 improper denials/year
weakened.why: The 13% (PA) and 18% (payment) figures match my recollection of OEI-09-18-00260 (250 PA and 250 payment denials sampled from 15 MAOs, one week of June 2019). The 'about 85,000 per year' figure is an extrapolation reported in press summaries and applies to the sampled MAOs, not all of MA; also the sample is one week in 2019 and predates CMS-4201-F. Weak as a measure of current 'conflict of authorities' volume.

weakened.claim: Premier: 15% initial denial rate, $57.23/denied claim, ~70% overturned, $25.7B/$18B
weakened.why: premierinc.com blocked. Premier's March 2024 release (516 hospitals) reported ~15% initial denials, $43.84 per claim and 54% of denials ultimately paid; the $57.23 / $25.7B / $18B figures are from a later Premier update I could not check, and the ~70% overturn rate does not match the 54% I recall from the 2024 release. Downgrade the overturn figure to unverified; note the '$18B potentially unnecessary' is Premier's administrative-waste estimate (cost of adjudicating claims that end up paid), not a cost of interpretive ambiguity.

weakened.claim: Change Healthcare Denials Index: registration/eligibility 26.6%, authorisation 11.6%, service not covered 10.6%, 86% avoidable
weakened.why: These percentages match the 2020 Denials Index (H1-2020 data) as I recall it; the 2022 index reports a similar front-end-dominated mix but I cannot confirm the exact figures are from the 2022 edition the finder cites. Vendor source either way. The direction (front-end/administrative causes dominate; medical necessity a minority) is robust across Change, Kodiak/Crowe and Experian surveys, so the H1 conclusion stands even if the edition is wrong.

weakened.claim: Orthopedics 2023 (PMID 37921528): near-100% P2P approval for orthopaedic CT/MRI denials
weakened.why: PubMed and Europe PMC blocked. Single-specialty, single-institution study; I could not confirm the sample size or exact rate. Directionally consistent with other P2P/appeal overturn data (KFF ~81%, OIG SNF), but 'nearly 100%' should not be generalised beyond advanced imaging in orthopaedics.

weakened.claim: JGIM 1996 survey: medical directors participate in policy review in 96% of plans, final authority in 27%
weakened.why: Unverifiable (PubMed blocked) and 30 years old (pre-MCG/InterQual dominance, pre-CMS-4201-F). It supports only the structural point that coverage policy is committee-owned; it says nothing about current volumes or process.

weakened.claim: AuthDenied CY2025 CMS-0057-F disclosure aggregation: median 7.2%, weighted 9.0%, 2.3-32.7% range, 6.2% appealed, 75.2% overturned
weakened.why: Vendor aggregator, blocked. The underlying disclosures are regulator-mandated, but the aggregation methodology (contract vs parent-org level, treatment of partial denials, whether pharmacy is included) is unverified. The 2.3-32.7% range, which the finder uses to argue variation is 'plan strategy', could partly reflect definitional differences between plans' reports. Use only as corroboration of the KFF order of magnitude.

weakened.claim: AHA Coding Clinic ~100 settlements per year industry-wide, 'tiny volume relative to disputes'
weakened.why: Published Q&A counts (28 in Q2 2025, 23 in Q2 2026) come from a blocked vendor blog and were extrapolated by the finder. The AHA Central Office also answers many inquiries individually without publishing them; the published count understates settlement activity but only published advice is authoritative. Direction (formal, prospective, low published volume) holds; the number is an estimate, not sourced.

weakened.claim: Payer-side $3.41 manual vs $0.05 automated per PA (HealthEdge citing CAQH); provider $10.97 vs $5.79 (CAQH 2024)
weakened.why: CAQH blocked. The provider figures are consistent with the CAQH Index series; the payer figures via a vendor blog are second-hand and the $0.05 'automated' figure refers to fully electronic transactions, not to interpretation. These are transaction-processing costs and say nothing about the cost of the ambiguous residue.

weakened.claim: Cohere Health 85-90% auto-approval; Waystar 6.8M payer rules; Alaffia $55M raise
weakened.why: All vendor or press. The finder flags them as vendor, correctly, but then uses them as evidence that approvals are 'already automated'. Vendor auto-approval rates are typically quoted for selected service lines with complete electronic submissions, not across the book. The stronger evidence for 'approvals automated, denials human' is the regulatory structure itself, not vendor claims.

weakened.claim: Texas gold card: settlement at provider level; uptake unconfirmed
weakened.why: texmed.org and tdi.texas.gov blocked. From background knowledge, TMA reported in 2023 that only about 3% of Texas physicians had received a gold-card exemption, prompting the 2025 amendments. If correct, this is evidence that even a statutory, data-driven prospective exemption mechanism produced negligible reuse in practice, which cuts against the idea that plans will readily let settled patterns bypass review.

weakened.claim: France DRSM Bretagne 64 médecins-conseils; CMRA 8,787 recours 2023; Cour des comptes 0.1% a-posteriori control
weakened.why: All from blocked pages/snippets, one from a law-firm blog. No national DAP volume was found, so the workflow's volume dimension is unknown, not low. The 'silence = acceptance' design is correctly described and is the decisive negative fact.

confirmed.claim: AHIP June-2025 report figures: 93% of commercial medical claims (96% of Rx) not subject to PA; 97-98% of medical PAs approved on final review; ~20% of medical PAs approved in real time; 45% of medical / 47% of Rx PA requests submitted manually; 'often a result of incomplete information from providers'; 100% of responding plans say AI without clinician review is not used to deny medical-necessity requests; commitment that all medical-necessity denials are reviewed by a licensed clinician ('reflects existing practices')
confirmed.evidence: PDF downloaded this session from https://ahiporg-production.s3.amazonaws.com/documents/202506_AHIP_Report_Prior_Authorization.pdf (industry association); text checked against the finder's saved extraction at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-sophon/03144a04-0e98-54e7-9d2c-78cb7b16e172/scratchpad/ahip_pa.txt. Survey base: October 2024, 32 commercial plans (51% of commercial enrolment), 21 Medicaid plans (53%), 21 MA plans (42%).

confirmed.claim: HL7 Da Vinci DTR expresses payer documentation rules as FHIR Questionnaires with embedded CQL logic and value sets; PAS defines FHIR-based PA submission
confirmed.evidence: Fetched https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HL7/davinci-dtr/master/input/pagecontent/index.md and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HL7/davinci-pas/master/input/pagecontent/index.md (standards body). Quote: 'DTR leverages FHIR Questionnaires combined with embedded CQL logic and associated value sets to retrieve existing information, prompt for additional relevant information, and manage the logic process.' Caveat the finder did not state: DTR/PAS adoption is mandated for impacted payers only from 1 Jan 2027 (CMS-0057-F), so executable payer rules are a standard, not yet common practice.

confirmed.claim: Regulatory structure: MA adverse medical-necessity determinations must be made by a physician or appropriate professional with expertise (42 CFR 422.566(d)); CMS-4201-F (422.101(b)(6), 422.137) requires internal coverage criteria used when Medicare criteria are 'not fully established' to be publicly accessible and evidence-based and reviewed annually by a UM committee; California SB 1120 (effective 1 Jan 2025) requires medical-necessity determinations to be made by a licensed physician or competent professional and bars AI from denying/delaying/modifying care on medical-necessity grounds
confirmed.evidence: Background knowledge of the regulations (govinfo, ecfr, leginfo all blocked this session); consistent with the AHIP text verified above. High confidence in the substance; treat exact CFR paragraph citations as unverified this session. Source types: regulator / legislature.

confirmed.claim: The settlement loop in this cluster exists but is institutionalised: payer medical policies with numbers, versions and effective dates; MCG/InterQual editions with plan customisation; LCD reconsideration and precedential Medicare Appeals Council decisions; AHA Coding Clinic quarterly authoritative advice
confirmed.evidence: Structure confirmed from background knowledge of each mechanism (payer documentation, CMS Program Integrity Manual ch.13, 42 CFR 401.109, AHA Central Office). Additional detail the finder missed: LCDs are operationalised by MACs as claims edits via Billing and Coding Articles with ICD-10/CPT code lists, so the regulator-level settlement is already executable, not merely published. Volume of precedential Council designations since the 2017 rule is, to my knowledge, in the single digits (unverified), which supports H2/H4: the Medicare appeals system deliberately adjudicates case by case.

confirmed.claim: Finder's classification that IMR (California DMHC and workers' comp) and OIG-documented appeal overturns are case-specific and non-precedential (prospective='no')
confirmed.evidence: Correct by design: California IMR decisions bind the plan for that enrollee only; workers' comp IMR applies the MTUS schedule per case. The contrast the finder draws (WC IMR overturn ~10% under a statutory treatment schedule vs ~70% under plan criteria) is a fair reading of the CA DIR and DMHC series as I know them, though exact figures are unverified this session. Additional point missed: California WC IMR volume is of the order of 100,000+ decisions per year (CA DIR annual reports, unverified), i.e. very high-volume criteria-bound review with essentially no precedent mechanism, which is itself evidence for H4 in a regulated medical-necessity setting.

manual_review_conflated_with_repeatable_: PA: the finder's H 3-8% for payer PA determinations is still too generous for a product. The residue it labels H ('criteria silent: new technology, off-label, not fully established') is by regulation routed into the medical-policy process (422.101(b)(6)/422.137) and is decided per case by a medical director until a policy exists (category E for the case, then policy authoring for the class). On the PA line itself, an operational settlement that changes future outcomes takes only two forms: (i) adding/removing a service from the PA list or an auto-approval rule (a bright-line change already handled by UM platforms and vendor 'policy digitisation'), or (ii) a customised criterion in MCG/InterQual (already versioned). Neither is an uncaptured interpretation. Honest H share for PA determinations as something a settlement-capture product could own: 0-3%, and for denials specifically 0% because the physician must decide every one (H4).

PA: the nurse-to-physician escalation is described as if it were an ambiguity escalation. In two-level UM the nurse refers when criteria are NOT met, not when criteria are unclear; the physician then exercises clinical judgment on the individual record (E) or confirms the criteria-not-met finding (B). Escalation volume is not an ambiguity signal.

PA: inter-insurer denial-rate dispersion (2.3-32.7%) is treated as 'plan policy choice' (good) but the finder still books a 25-35% 'B factual classification' share as if it were clean criteria matching; much of that matching is done against plan-customised criteria that the plan could relax at will, i.e. the human labour is a consequence of a commercial coverage stance, not of under-specified rules.

Medical policy formation: labelled H 40-60%, but deciding a coverage position for a class of technology is policy authoring (generating the rule), which the brief's section 1 explicitly excludes from the mechanism ('does NOT primarily generate policy text'). The H that remains is the interpretation of an existing NCD/LCD or MCG guideline for edge cases (finder's C/D, 25-45%), and that is captured today as policy addenda and customisation documents. H as defined by the brief: 10-25%, and already encoded (H3).

Claims denials: H 5-15% is booked for E/M leveling, modifier 25/59, sepsis validation and inpatient status. On the provider side these are interpretations owned by the counterparty (the payer) or by industry bodies (CPT Assistant, Coding Clinic, NCCI, two-midnight rule); the provider cannot 'settle' them, only learn and argue them. That fails the brief's 'clear institutional owner who can approve interpretations' test and is closer to knowledge management of external rules. Inpatient-status secondary review is per-patient clinical judgment (E). Honest provider-side H: 0-5%. Payer-side H (deciding how the plan reads a coding rule) is real but is already run as versioned payment-policy/edit libraries (Cotiviti, ClaimsXten, Optum CES), i.e. H3.

P2P: correctly scored H <5%; the finder's A 50-70% is directionally right but the P2P overturn rate partly reflects physician-to-physician deference and payer reluctance to litigate, not only missing evidence; some of that share belongs to E, none to H. No change to verdict.

General: the finder counts a policy that is published and versioned as a 'settlement loop' even where no operational system consumes it (e.g., the JGIM 1996 committee description, Anthem ADMIN.00001 existence-only, PacificSource/Priority Health titles). Existence of a document does not show a case-to-policy loop with reuse; the finder itself notes the per-case ledger is unevidenced. These items should be read as evidence of H3 (already encoded) rather than of an unmet capture need.

corrected_workflow_verdicts.name: Prior authorisation medical-necessity determinations (payer side, US Medicare Advantage + commercial)
corrected_workflow_verdicts.why: Volume is real (KFF ~53M MA determinations, unverified this session) but the human labour is criteria matching and record review (A/B) plus physician judgment on criteria-not-met cases (E). Every medical-necessity denial must be made by a licensed clinician (AHIP text verified; 42 CFR 422.566(d); SB 1120), so precedent cannot displace the reviewer in the only decision class where interpretation lives (H4). Recurring gaps in criteria are, by regulation, routed into public, annually reviewed internal coverage criteria and MCG/InterQual customisation (H3). The finder's own 80% human-touch and 4.2M physician-decision figures are inferences that overstate the pool. Evidence quality downgraded from strong to moderate because every load-bearing number except AHIP's rests on blocked-page snippets.

corrected_workflow_verdicts.name: Payer medical policy / clinical coverage policy formation and maintenance
corrected_workflow_verdicts.why: This is where recurring ambiguity is settled prospectively, but the work is coverage-policy authoring by committees (excluded by the brief's mechanism definition), volume is hundreds of policies per plan with cadence monthly-quarterly (unquantified), the labour pool is a small medical-policy team per plan (H8), and outputs are already numbered, versioned, effective-dated and, under CMS-4201-F, publicly posted and annually reviewed (H3). The only unevidenced gap is a case-to-policy ledger, and nothing found shows anyone pays for its absence. Downgraded from uncertain to weak; evidence quality weak because the process sources (Anthem ADMIN.00001, PacificSource, Priority Health, JGIM 1996) were unreadable or 30 years old.

corrected_workflow_verdicts.name: Claims edits, denials and appeals (provider-payer, US)
corrected_workflow_verdicts.why: Denial causes are dominated by front-end/administrative and documentation issues (Change Healthcare index; Premier), the interpretive residue (sepsis, E/M, modifiers, status) is settled by the payer unilaterally (versioned payment policies and edit libraries, H3), by industry bodies at low volume (Coding Clinic, CPT Assistant, NCCI), by regulation (two-midnight) or bilaterally in contracts (F). The provider is not the owner of the interpretation, so a provider-side 'payer playbook' is knowledge management of external rules, not the settlement loop. The sepsis item was a journal proposal, not an observed settlement. Overturn and cost figures from Premier could not be verified and the 70% overturn rate conflicts with the 54% in Premier's 2024 release. Downgraded from uncertain to weak.

corrected_workflow_verdicts.name: Peer-to-peer reviews and appeals of PA denials (provider vs payer medical director)
corrected_workflow_verdicts.why: Agree with the finder. Outcomes are explicitly non-precedential (IMR, MA reconsiderations, ALJ appeals with single-digit precedential designations since 2017), physician-to-physician by law, and driven by record supply and clinical judgment. Additional negative evidence: even the statutory, data-driven Texas gold-card mechanism produced ~3% physician uptake in 2023 (TMA, background knowledge, unverified), showing plans do not readily let settled patterns bypass per-case review.

corrected_workflow_verdicts.name: France: CPAM/MSA accord préalable (entente préalable) and service médical avis
corrected_workflow_verdicts.why: Agree with the finder. Deemed approval by silence (15/21 days) means the only decisions are refusals by médecins-conseils; recurring classes are settled nationally by HAS référentiels and MSAP thresholds, i.e. by the regulator, not by a local owner; single public buyer; national volumes unknown. All French figures come from blocked pages or a law-firm blog.

missing: State-level H4 reinforcement beyond California: many state UR statutes already require a physician (often same-specialty) for adverse determinations, and 2025-2026 state AI-in-UR laws (e.g., Arizona HB 2175 requiring individual medical-director review of AI-flagged denials; similar bills in Maryland, Nebraska and others) extend the human-must-decide rule nationally. The finder cites only SB 1120 and CMS; the constraint is broader and tightening.

CMS WISeR model (traditional Medicare, from January 2026, six states): CMS itself contracts technology vendors to apply PA criteria for selected services while requiring that any denial be made by a licensed clinician. This is the regulator institutionalising 'automate criteria matching, keep humans on denials', which is direct evidence that the addressable layer is B automation already being procured, not H capture.

Plans' actual settlement mechanism for recurring approvals is list removal, not interpretation capture: UnitedHealthcare's 2024 national gold-card programme, Cigna's removal of ~25% of PA codes, and the AHIP commitment (verified text) to 'individually reduce the volume of in-network medical prior authorizations by January 1, 2026'. When a class is reliably approved, the bright line moves; that is the IPSA finding again (repetition governed by bright lines, disputes at the tail).

OIG 2022 detail cutting against H1-as-provider-fault: OIG found MAOs requested documentation that was already in the file and made reviewer errors; some of the 'missing evidence' is payer-imposed, which is neither H nor a capture problem.

Provider-side documentation labour that the finder omitted: clinical documentation integrity (CDI) query programmes generate very high query volumes (query rates commonly 20-30% of inpatient discharges, vendor/industry benchmarks) and are the true home of the sepsis/clinical-validation issue; that labour is category A/B (getting the physician to document), not H.

Medicare FFS appeals as a natural experiment: the OMHA ALJ backlog (hundreds of thousands of pending appeals mid-2010s; healthdata.gov and hhs.gov blocked) coexists with a precedential mechanism (42 CFR 401.109) that has been used only a handful of times. The system with the most repeated medical-necessity disputes in the country chose not to build precedent into operations. Strong H4/H2 evidence the finder only touched.

Da Vinci adoption timing: DTR/PAS/CRD are mandated only from 2027 and adoption is early, so 'payer rules as executable CQL' is a standard not a deployed base. This weakens the finder's H3 argument slightly but the gap is being filled by mandated APIs and incumbent vendors (Availity, Epic Payer Platform, Cohere), not by a settlement ledger.

No verification possible this session for: KFF 2024 counts, OIG 2026 SNF/LTCH/IRF reports, Premier update figures, Orthopedics 2023 P2P study, JGIM 1996, AuthDenied aggregation, CA IMR counts, Coding Clinic volumes, Texas gold-card uptake, French figures. Each remains unverified; none was found to be contradicted by other evidence except the Premier overturn rate.
verification.overall: The finder's conclusion (weak cluster, do not pick as wedge) survives verification and should be strengthened, not softened. The one load-bearing source I could read in full (AHIP June 2025) checks out exactly: 7% of commercial medical claims subject to PA, 97-98% approved, ~20% real-time, 45% manual, and an explicit, already-in-effect commitment that every medical-necessity denial is clinician-reviewed. The finder overreached in three places: inferring an 80% human-touch rate from the 20% real-time figure, treating all ~4.2M MA denials as physician decisions, and booking a journal proposal (Sepsis-2.5) and bilateral contract terms as settlement-loop evidence. It also gave the medical-policy workflow an H share of 40-60% when that work is coverage-policy authoring, which the brief excludes from the mechanism, and is already numbered, versioned, effective-dated and, under CMS-4201-F, public and annually reviewed. Re-estimated honest H shares: PA determinations 0-3% (0% for denials), medical policy 10-25% but fully encoded, claims 0-5% on the provider side. Every settlement loop found is either regulator-owned (CMS-4201-F, two-midnight, LCDs with executable billing articles, HAS référentiels), industry-owned (Coding Clinic, CPT Assistant), vendor-owned (payment-policy edit libraries, MCG/InterQual editions), or bilateral-commercial (contract definitions); none is an uncaptured institutional interpretation sitting in email and spreadsheets. Evidence the finder missed all cuts the same way: state AI-in-UR laws and CMS's own WISeR model keep humans on denials while automating criteria matching; plans settle recurring approvals by removing services from PA lists (bright lines) rather than capturing interpretations; the Medicare appeals system, the largest repeated medical-necessity dispute machine in the country, uses its precedential mechanism only a handful of times. Corrected verdicts: PA determinations negative, medical policy weak, claims weak, P2P negative, France negative. Caveat: because WebSearch was exhausted and the egress proxy blocked all non-GitHub hosts, most numeric checks rest on my background knowledge of the cited primary sources; I found one likely inconsistency (Premier ~70% vs 54% overturn) and no evidence that any cited number was invented.
